title: DATA 322: Machine Learning for Data Science
text:
Course Overview
DATA 322: Machine Learning for Data Science (4 units) provides a broad introduction to machine learning, data mining, and statistical pattern recognition. Topics include supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and best practices in machine learning, with a practical emphasis on real-world applications.
Lecture: Monday, Wednesday, Friday, 1:00–1:50 PM, BSS 408
Lab: Tuesday, 1:00–2:50 PM, BSS 313
Program Requirement: Required for the Data Science major

title: DATA 322: Machine Learning for Data Science
text:
Course Structure
Includes daily warm-up problems during lecture, weekly programming labs, weekly quizzes during lab sessions, two major projects (Unsupervised Learning and Supervised Learning), one midterm exam, and a comprehensive final exam. Projects allow students to apply machine learning techniques to real data problems and may be used as part of a professional portfolio.

title: Lecture 16
text:
Distinguish between supervised and unsupervised learning.
Distinguish among descriptive, predictive, estimation, and testing analyses; use random-variable vs. summary notation; and recognize confounding and control for bias in estimation and testing.
Use appropriate notation to describe a supervised learning problem (available dataset, hypothetical dataset, true relationship, predicted relationship, predicted target, training data, test data).
State the bias–variance decomposition of the expected test error.
Classify a supervised learning problem as regression or classification.
Explain flexibility of a model and its role in the bias–variance trade-off.
Explain interpretability of a model and when it matters.





Supervised learning: Imagine we have a response (or outcome, target) variable \(Y\) that we want to predict. Imagine we have one or more features (predictors or inputs) \(X_1, \ldots, X_p\) that might provide information to improve the prediction. The goal of supervised learning is to learn a function that maps the features to the response, using a labeled dataset where values of \(Y\) are recorded along with values of the features for a set of examples. Two main tasks are regression (when \(Y\) is quantitative) and classification (when \(Y\) is categorical).
Unsupervised learning: We observe only features \(X_1, \ldots, X_p\); there is no response variable. The goal is to find structure in the data,e.g., groups (clustering), low-dimensional summaries, or associations—without a target to predict.
Example 1: Predict building-level energy use (regression) or whether a site is suitable for solar (classification) from building and location features. Unsupervised: cluster neighborhoods by energy use, renewables, and transport to design targeted sustainability programs.
Example 2: Predict next quarter’s sales (regression) or whether a customer will churn (classification) from purchase history and demographics. Unsupervised: segment customers by spending, frequency, and product mix for targeted marketing.
Example 3: Predict weekly candy sales per store (regression) or whether a new product will be a top seller (classification) from price, shelf position, and store type. Unsupervised: cluster candy SKUs by sugar content, size, and price point to design product lines or store layouts.
Example 4: Predict length of stay or readmission risk (regression or classification) from vitals, labs, and demographics. Unsupervised: cluster patients by diagnoses, procedures, and utilization to identify care pathways or risk strata.




Data analyses can be classified into four types. Using random variable vs. summary notation helps keep the goal clear: we use capital letters (e.g. \(X\), \(Y\)) for random variables and symbols like \(\bar{x}\), \(\hat{\beta}\), or population parameters \(\mu\), \(\beta\) for summaries or quantities we estimate/test.
Descriptive (what’s in the dataset I have): Summarize the observed dataset only with no formal notion of a larger population or future individuals. We describe the data at hand.
Predictive (a guess for an individual’s value): For a specific unit (e.g., a new customer, next week’s total sales, a new patient), we want to predict that unit’s outcome. Notation: for a new or future unit we have inputs \(X^0\) and want to predict the random variable \(Y^0\); our guess is \(\hat{Y}^0 = \hat{f}(X^0)\). The focus is on accuracy of the predicted value for that unit: mere correlation between inputs and output is fine.
Estimation (What is the summary of a population or relationship?): We want to know summary that describes a population or a relationship (e.g., population mean \(\mu\), average treatment effect) but have only data from a subset of the population. Notation: population quantities are parameters/quantities that are fixed (as opposed to random variables) (e.g. \(\mu\), \(\beta\)); we can estimate them with sample-based estimators \(\hat{\mu}\), \(\hat{\beta}\) and report confidence intervals. If we are estimating a relationship or treatment effect, confounding can bias our estimate (this is when a third variable influences both the predictor (or treatment) and the outcome) so the raw association does not equal the causal effect. We can control for confounders (e.g., by “adjusting” for them, or by study design such as randomized control trials) so that the estimated relationship is less biased. Causal diagrams (DAGs) help identify which variables to condition on: we typically need to adjust for variables that cause both treatment and outcome (backdoor paths) to avoid bias.
Testing (is the summary or relationship in the population different from…?): We ask whether a population quantity or relationship differs from a benchmark (e.g., zero, a null value) based on data from a subset of the population. Notation: we state a null hypothesis about a parameter (e.g. \(H_0: \beta = 0\)) and use the sample to compute a test statistic and \(p\)-value. Causal/confounding: The same confounding issues as in estimation apply: if we test “does \(X\) affect \(Y\)?” without controlling for confounders, the test can be misleading (e.g., significant only because of confounding, or non-significant because we did not control and the effect is masked). Controlling for bias via appropriate adjustment or design is part of valid testing when the goal is to learn about a population relationship or causal effect.
Example 1: Describe average emissions and correlation with income in the sample (descriptive). Predict next week’s demand for the grid (predictive). Estimate how much rooftop solar reduces emissions in the population, controlling for income and region to limit confounding (estimation). Test whether the population effect of solar on emissions is different from zero (testing).
Example 2: Describe mean sales and distribution by region in the data (descriptive). Predict next month’s demand for a specific store (predictive). Estimate how much a 10% price increase reduces unit sales in the population, controlling for season and store type (estimation). Test whether that effect differs from zero (testing).
Example 3: Describe candy sales and price in the sample (descriptive). Predict Halloween demand by store (predictive). Estimate how much shelf placement affects sales in the population, controlling for store size and promotion (estimation). Test whether the effect of placement is zero (testing).
Example 4: Describe readmission rate and lab values in the sample (descriptive). Predict which patient will need ICU in 24 hours (predictive). Estimate how much a care bundle reduces readmission in the population, controlling for severity and comorbidities to limit confounding (estimation). Test whether the treatment effect is different from zero (testing).




In ISL style:

Available (training) data: \(n\) examples\(\{(x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)\}\), often written as design matrix \(X\) and response vector \(y\). Together these form the training dataset \(S\). More than one feature can be used, in which case each \(x_i\) is a vector of length \(p\)
True relationship: \(Y = f(X) + \varepsilon\), where \(f\) is the unknown true function and \(\varepsilon\) is irreducible error.
Estimated (predicted) relationship: \(\hat{f}(X)\), learned from the training data.
Predicted value: \(\hat{Y} = \hat{f}(X)\) for a given \(X\) (training or new).
Hypothetical (test) data: New pairs \((X^0, Y^0)\) not used to fit \(\hat{f}\); used to evaluate prediction error, e.g. \(\text{E}[(Y^0 - \hat{f}(X^0))^2]\).

Example 1: \(Y\) = annual CO₂ emissions per capita; \(X\) = GDP per capita, energy mix, population density, policy indices. We fit \(\hat{f}\) on country-year data; the “hypothetical” set might be future years or held-out countries to assess generalizability of emission predictions.
Example 2: \(Y\) = revenue per customer; \(X\) = tenure, product count, support tickets, region. We fit \(\hat{f}\) on historical accounts; the hypothetical set might be next quarter or a held-out region to evaluate revenue forecasts.
Example 3: \(Y\) = candy sales (units or revenue) per store-week; \(X\) = price, shelf position, season, store size, promotion. We fit \(\hat{f}\) on past store-weeks; the hypothetical set might be next quarter or held-out stores to evaluate demand forecasts.
Example 4: \(Y\) = readmission within 30 days or blood glucose level; \(X\) = labs, vitals, medications, demographics, prior visits. We fit \(\hat{f}\) on historical patients; the hypothetical set might be future admissions or held-out hospitals to evaluate risk or outcome predictions.




For squared-error loss and a fixed test input \(X^0\), the expected test error (expectation over training sets) is:
\[
\text{E}\bigl[(Y^0 - \hat{f}(X^0))^2\bigr] = \underbrace{\text{Var}(\varepsilon)}_{\text{irreducible}} + \underbrace{\bigl[\text{E}[\hat{f}(X^0)] - f(X^0)\bigr]^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} + \underbrace{\text{Var}(\hat{f}(X^0))}_{\text{Variance}}
\]
If \(X^0\) is random (e.g., drawn from the same distribution as future inputs), we take expectation over both the training set and \(X^0\). That adds an outer \(\text{E}_{X^0}\): the expected test error becomes \(\text{E}_{X^0}\bigl[\text{E}[(Y^0 - \hat{f}(X^0))^2 \mid X^0]\bigr]\), and the same decomposition holds given \(X^0\), so we just average the right-hand side over the distribution of \(X^0\).

Irreducible error: Noise in \(Y\) that cannot be reduced by better modeling.
Bias: Systematic error from approximating \(f\) by a simpler or restricted \(\hat{f}\); often high when the model is too rigid (underfitting).
Variance: Variability of \(\hat{f}\) across different training samples; often high when the model is too flexible (overfitting).

Example 1: Predicting crop yield under climate change: a very simple model (bias-dominated) may miss nonlinear effects of temperature and water; a very complex model (variance-dominated) may overfit to a few regions.
Example 2: Predicting candy demand: a simple model may miss Halloween and holiday spikes; an overly flexible model may overfit to one year’s promotions and not generalize well to future promotions.
Example 3: Predicting readmission risk: a simple model may miss interactions between conditions and social determinants; an overly flexible model may overfit to one hospital’s coding or population.




Regression: The response \(Y\) is quantitative (continuous or discrete numeric). We predict a number (e.g., energy use, temperature, emissions). Typical loss: squared error; metrics: RMSE, MAE, \(R^2\).
Classification: The response \(Y\) is categorical (e.g., yes/no, land-use type). We predict a class. Typical loss: 0–1 loss or cross-entropy; metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, AUC.
Example 1: Regression: predict tons of CO₂ sequestered per hectare from forest type, age, and climate. Classification: classify satellite imagery into forest / agriculture / urban to monitor deforestation or urban sprawl.
Example 2: Regression: predict daily demand or delivery time from season, promotions, and store features. Classification: classify leads as likely-to-convert vs not, or transactions as fraudulent vs legitimate.
Example 3: Regression: predict sugar content (g per serving) or sales from ingredients, price, and package size. Classification: classify candy as chocolate / fruit / nut / other, or as “kid-focused” vs “adult” for shelf placement.
Example 4: Regression: predict length of stay or blood glucose from vitals, labs, and medications. Classification: classify patients as high-risk vs low-risk for readmission, or diagnose disease category from symptoms and lab results.




Flexibility is the capacity of a model to fit different shapes of the input–output relationship. Low flexibility (e.g., linear model): smooth, stable fits, but may miss curvature and interactions (high bias, low variance). High flexibility (e.g., deep trees, many predictors): can fit complex and nonlinear patterns, but may overfit (low bias, high variance). Tuning (e.g., regularization, tree depth) controls flexibility and the bias–variance trade-off.
Example 1: Modeling species presence from climate and land use: a linear model may be too rigid; a flexible model can capture thresholds and interactions (e.g., temperature × rainfall) but may not generalize well.
Example 2: Modeling conversion rate from ad spend and demographics: a linear model may miss saturation effects and segment-specific response; a very flexible model may overfit to short campaigns.
Example 3: Modeling candy preference or sales from sugar content and type: a linear model may miss a “sweet spot” (preference peaks at moderate sugar); a very flexible model may overfit to a few brands.
Example 4: Modeling treatment response or disease progression from biomarkers and demographics: a linear model may miss dose–response thresholds or subgroup effects; a very flexible model may overfit to a single site or cohort.




Interpretability is the ease with which a human can understand how the model uses inputs to form predictions or conclusions. Interpretable models (e.g., linear regression, small trees, additive models) allow one to inspect coefficients, variable importance, or simple rules. Black-box models (e.g., large ensembles, deep nets) may be more accurate but harder to explain.
Example 1: An interpretable model might show: “each additional kW of rooftop solar is associated with an average reduction of \(X\) kg CO₂/year, holding income constant”—useful for communication and policy. A black-box model might predict grid stability better but be hard to explain to regulators or the public.

This course provides a broad introduction to machine learning, data mining, and statistical pattern recognition. Topics include supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and best practices in machine learning. The course draws from numerous case studies and applications, with a practical rather than theoretical emphasis.
Weekly: Lecture 3 hrs. Activity 2 hrs.
Prerequisites: DATA 271, MATH 107, STAT 109
A minimum grade of C- is required for the course to count toward the Data Science major.




(Note, students can find program learning outcomes on the program website, and institution learning outcomes here: https://academicprograms.humboldt.edu/content/baccalaureate-student-learning-outcomes)
(1) Students will demonstrate computational skills to extract different types and quantities of data from multiple sources and create visualizations and other data products for various audiences. (ILO 3,4,7)
In order to achieve PLO 1, students will demonstrate the following specific measurable behaviors:

(SLO 1) Students will extract quantitative and categorical data from a large public database, calculate relevant summary statistics, and present findings numerically and graphically for in-class individual and group data projects.

(2) Students will demonstrate statistical knowledge to build mathematical models and ensure the validity of data and its analysis. (ILO 7)
In order to achieve PLO 2, students will demonstrate the following specific measurable behaviors:

(SLO 2) Students will design a mathematical (logic) model to guide analysis and ensure valid and reliable results for in-class individual and group data projects.

(5) Students will communicate effectively with a diverse range of audiences. (ILO 5,6)
In order to achieve PLO 5, students will demonstrate the following specific measurable behaviors:

(SLO 5a) Students will prepare a written description of a mathematical model in which they explain the context, describe their methodology, analyze their data, and reach a conclusion that includes a discussion of its implications.

Additionally, one of students’ two projects, communicated in written form, will be the application of Machine Learning algorithms (supervised and unsupervised, respectively) to a data set related to one of the following: sustainability, social justice, or Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK). This project supports ILOs (1) and (2).




By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Recognize the characteristics of machine learning that make it useful for real-world problems.
Explain how machine learning differs from inferential statistical modeling.
Characterize machine learning algorithms as supervised and unsupervised.
Implement common machine learning algorithms using Python-based toolkits.
Apply regression, classification, and clustering methods to real data sets.
Evaluate model performance and select appropriate models based on context and goals.
Communicate modeling choices, results, and limitations to a variety of audiences.
Identify and discuss ethical considerations related to data collection, modeling, and algorithmic decision-making.





This course supports the Data Science Program Learning Outcomes and Cal Poly Humboldt’s Institutional Learning Outcomes related to quantitative reasoning, critical thinking, communication, and ethical reasoning.




DATA 322 includes:

Three weekly lecture meetings
One weekly laboratory session

In this 4-unit course, students should expect to spend approximately 12 hours per week on course-related work. This includes time in lecture (3 hours), lab time (2 hours), and time outside of class to complete readings, assignments, projects, and exam preparation (approximately 7 hours).




Textbook:
An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in Python
Available free online or for purchase in print.
Software:
Python and commonly used data science libraries (installed on all campus computers)
Other Technology:
Regular access to a computer with reliable internet
Students without personal access to required technology may use campus computer labs and library resources.




Students enter DATA 322 with different backgrounds in statistics, mathematics, and programming. That’s expected. You do not need to be an expert at the start of the semester to succeed in this course. What matters most is steady engagement and a willingness to practice, reflect, and ask questions.
Students who are successful in this course typically:

Attend lecture and lab regularly.
Class time is used to build intuition, practice ideas, and work through examples that are difficult to learn independently.
Participate actively in daily warm-ups.
Warm-ups are designed to help you engage with your classmates and develop conceptual understanding and confidence before moving to more complex problems.
Use labs as a space to practice and make mistakes.
Labs are meant for learning, not perfection. Comparing your work to posted results and reflecting on differences is an important part of the learning process.
Prepare consistently for weekly quizzes.
Quizzes are short and predictable, but they require regular practice. Reviewing lecture notes, lab activities, and assigned textbook problems each week will help you succeed.
Start projects early and work iteratively.
Projects are most successful when you begin early, test ideas incrementally, and seek feedback along the way. I’ve deliberately chosen two projects that reflect significant problems with real applications of ML. At first glance, the datasets might appear simple but great care is required to build useful products out of them. Rather than tell you a solution to implement, I’m going to use our class time to guide class discussions so that students will be active participants in creating appropriate solutions.
Collaborate appropriately with classmates.
Discussing ideas and approaches is encouraged, but all submitted work must reflect your own understanding unless otherwise specified.
Ask for help when you need it.
If you are struggling with course material, please reach out during office hours, lab sessions, or by email. Seeking help early can make a significant difference.

As a general guideline, you should plan to spend approximately three hours per week per unit on course-related work, including time in class and time outside of class. For this 4-unit course, this corresponds to about 12 hours per week total. Individual experiences will vary, but this can be a helpful frame of reference when planning your time.




Students will complete a variety of assessments designed to support regular practice, provide regular feedback, and evaluate mastery of machine learning concepts and methods.
Assessments in this course include:

Daily warm-up problems during lecture (Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays).
These short activities are designed to help students engage with new concepts, build intuition, and practice explaining ideas with peers. Warm-ups are graded on participation.
Weekly programming labs.
Labs provide guided, hands-on practice implementing machine learning methods using Python. Labs are intended as formative learning experiences. I’ll provide desired outputs so students can check their work and reflect on their understanding before turning in their work. Labs will be graded on completion.
Early in the semester, you will complete a mini project as part of the weekly labs. This project introduces the full workflow of an applied machine learning task in a simplified and supported setting. Using a provided Google Colab notebook, the class will modify an existing recommender system to form study groups based on survey responses collected from real participants.
The goal of this mini project is not to produce perfect groupings, but to practice:

Designing questions that can be translated into quantitative features
Explore distance metrics
Applying and interpreting clustering algorithms
Working collaboratively with a shared product
Reflecting on modeling decisions and their consequences

This experience is designed to make the larger course projects more approachable and to build confidence before tackling more complex open-ended problems.
Weekly quizzes during lab sessions.
Quizzes assess understanding of both lab material and assigned practice problems. Quiz questions may include conceptual questions, mathematical calculations, interpretation of output or visualizations, and short problem-solving tasks. Quizzes are designed to encourage steady preparation and synthesis of ideas.
Two projects.
Projects require students to apply machine learning methods to real data, justify modeling choices, evaluate performance, and communicate results in written form. Projects emphasize modeling choices, interpretation, and communication and may be used as part of a professional portfolio.

Unsupervised Learning Project:
In this project, you will use unsupervised learning techniques to build a major recommender system for Cal Poly Humboldt using publicly available data. The goal is to explore and justify modeling choices, and communicate the resulting recommendations clearly and responsibly.
Supervised Learning Project:
In this project, you will work with data from a one-dimensional simulation of a fusion reactor to develop a model to predict the onset of instabilities before they occur. This project emphasizes feature engineering, computational efficiency and valid model evaluation in an effort to help further research in California’s renewable energy sector.

One midterm exam and one final exam.

title: Resources
text:
This course provides a broad introduction to machine learning, data mining, and statistical pattern recognition. Topics include supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and best practices in machine learning. The course draws from numerous case studies and applications, with a practical rather than theoretical emphasis.
Weekly: Lecture 3 hrs. Activity 2 hrs.
Prerequisites: DATA 271, MATH 107, STAT 109
A minimum grade of C- is required for the course to count toward the Data Science major.

title: Resources
text:
(Note, students can find program learning outcomes on the program website, and institution learning outcomes here: https://academicprograms.humboldt.edu/content/baccalaureate-student-learning-outcomes)
(1) Students will demonstrate computational skills to extract different types and quantities of data from multiple sources and create visualizations and other data products for various audiences. (ILO 3,4,7)
In order to achieve PLO 1, students will demonstrate the following specific measurable behaviors:

(SLO 1) Students will extract quantitative and categorical data from a large public database, calculate relevant summary statistics, and present findings numerically and graphically for in-class individual and group data projects.

(2) Students will demonstrate statistical knowledge to build mathematical models and ensure the validity of data and its analysis. (ILO 7)
In order to achieve PLO 2, students will demonstrate the following specific measurable behaviors:

(SLO 2) Students will design a mathematical (logic) model to guide analysis and ensure valid and reliable results for in-class individual and group data projects.

(5) Students will communicate effectively with a diverse range of audiences. (ILO 5,6)
In order to achieve PLO 5, students will demonstrate the following specific measurable behaviors:

(SLO 5a) Students will prepare a written description of a mathematical model in which they explain the context, describe their methodology, analyze their data, and reach a conclusion that includes a discussion of its implications.

Additionally, one of students’ two projects, communicated in written form, will be the application of Machine Learning algorithms (supervised and unsupervised, respectively) to a data set related to one of the following: sustainability, social justice, or Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK). This project supports ILOs (1) and (2).

Linux: Install via your distribution’s package manager or from python.org



Python Data Science Libraries
Commonly used libraries for this course include: - numpy - Numerical computing - pandas - Data manipulation and analysis - scikit-learn - Machine learning algorithms - matplotlib - Data visualization - seaborn - Statistical data visualization
Install via pip: pip install numpy pandas scikit-learn matplotlib seaborn


Python in Google Colab
Access Python in Google Colab: Google Colab
Google Colab provides free access to Python in a cloud-based notebook environment with many data science libraries pre-installed. This is useful if you don’t want to install Python on your computer or need to work from different devices.


Python in Jupyter Notebook
Install Jupyter: Jupyter Installation Guide
Jupyter Notebook is a popular environment for interactive Python development and data analysis.

Install Python first
Install Jupyter: pip install jupyter
Launch Jupyter: jupyter notebook

Note: Python and commonly used data science libraries are installed on all campus computers, so you can use the computer labs if you prefer not to install software on your personal computer.
